label: TMUA 2023 · Paper 2 · Question 6
knowledgePattern: Check reversible logarithms, squaring and a bijective input rescaling
solution:
Any solution of ax=x has x>0. Taking logarithms to base a>1 is reversible, so statement I has exactly the same solutions.

In II, a2x=x2 means ax=|x|. In addition to the original positive solutions it has a negative solution: for x=−1, ax+x=1/a−1<0, whereas at x=0 it equals 1. This function is strictly increasing, so it crosses zero exactly once between them. That extra solution cannot solve the original equation.

In III, set u=2x. The equation becomes au=u; since x↦2x is one-to-one and covers all real inputs, the number of solutions is unchanged.

I and III only: answer F.

hints.title: Keep the allowed domain
hints.body: Use the sign of ax to establish the domain of any original solution before taking a logarithm.
hints.recap: Logarithms are defined for positive arguments, and taking a logarithm with a valid base reverses exponentiation.
hints.pitfall: A transformed equation must be checked for solutions outside the original domain.
hints.pause: Compare the original equation with I in both directions.

recall.reminder: Logarithms are defined for positive arguments, and taking a logarithm with a valid base reverses exponentiation.

hints.title: Reverse a square carefully
hints.body: When an equation equates two squares, write both possible signs before counting its roots.
hints.recap: Squaring can introduce solutions, so reverse steps require their sign conditions.
hints.pitfall: Do not replace a principal square root of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></math> by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> without checking its sign.
hints.pause: Examine each sign case in II, including negative inputs.

recall.reminder: Squaring can introduce solutions, so reverse steps require their sign conditions.

hints.title: Rename the whole input
hints.body: For III use a new variable for the complete exponent, and compare how its possible inputs correspond to the old ones.
hints.recap: A nonzero horizontal rescaling changes input locations through a one-to-one correspondence.
hints.pitfall: The same number of roots does not mean the roots occur at the same inputs.
hints.pause: Determine whether each equation preserves the number of solutions, then choose the correct statements.

recall.reminder: A nonzero horizontal rescaling changes input locations through a one-to-one correspondence.
